introduction_markdown:
Multiple choice paper (0780 Physics 1, June 2021, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one you score zero). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. The use of a calculator and the Formulae book is allowed.

**Constants used in the answers** (the paper itself prints no data sheet): acceleration of free fall $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (question 24 gives the same result with $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$); specific heat capacity of water $4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ (question 32).

**Section I (thirty five questions), Questions 1-35.** Directions: Each of the questions or incomplete statements in this section is followed by four suggested answers. Select the best answer in each case.

**Section II (ten questions), Multiple Selection, Questions 36-45.** Directions: for each of the questions or incomplete statements in this section ONE or TWO of the responses given is/are correct. Decide which of the response(s) is/are correct. Then choose: A - if 1 and 2 are correct; B - if 2 and 3 are correct; C - if 1 only is correct; D - if 3 only is correct. (Directions summarised: A = 1, 2 only; B = 2, 3 only; C = 1 only; D = 3 only.)

**Section III (five questions), Questions 46-50.** Directions: Each of the questions (46-50) has four sets of graphs A-D. Which of the graphs in each question best fits the relationship between $x$ and $y$?

questions.enonce_markdown: Equality or equivalence in units for all terms in a physical equation makes the equation
questions.corrige_markdown:
Having the same units (dimensions) on both sides and in every term is the test of **homogeneity**. It is a necessary condition, but it is not sufficient: dimensionless numerical factors (for example the $\frac12$ in $s=ut+\frac12at^2$) and dimensionless functions cannot be checked this way, so a homogeneous equation may still be wrong.

- A: false, homogeneity does not guarantee that the equation is physically correct.
- B and C: "homogeneous only" and "physically correct only" are not acceptable descriptions (a correct equation is always homogeneous).
- D: an equation that passes the unit test is homogeneous and *possibly* correct.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The resultant force acting on object, P, in figure 1 is;

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take East as $+x$ and North as $+y$. The forces are $100.0\ \mathrm{N}$ East, $40.0\ \mathrm{N}$ West (figure shows the arrow pointing left) and $80.0\ \mathrm{N}$ North.

- Horizontal component: $100.0-40.0=60.0\ \mathrm{N}$ East.
- Vertical component: $80.0\ \mathrm{N}$ North.

Magnitude: $R=\sqrt{60.0^2+80.0^2}=100.0\ \mathrm{N}$. Direction: $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{80.0}{60.0}\right)=53.1^\circ$ North of East, that is in the North-East quadrant.

Option A is the only one with a resultant of $100.0\ \mathrm{N}$ in the North-East direction. B uses only the vertical force, C only the net horizontal force and D has neither the right size nor the right direction.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: 100.0 N, North East of position of P
80.0 N, due North of position of P
60.0 N, due East of position of P
40.0 N, South East of position of P

questions.enonce_markdown:
A system which can attain resonance

*Options as printed:* A) oscillates with large amplitude   B) oscillates at its natural frequency   C) encounters very little damping   D) performs forced oscillations
questions.corrige_markdown:
Resonance is the large-amplitude response of an oscillating system when it is driven by a periodic external force whose frequency equals the natural frequency of the system.

- A describes the *result* of resonance, not a property that a system must have beforehand.
- C: light damping makes the resonance peak taller and sharper, but resonance still occurs (with a smaller amplitude) in a damped system.
- B: every oscillating system has a natural frequency and oscillates at it when it is left to vibrate freely, but free oscillation is not resonance.
- D: resonance is a phenomenon of **forced oscillations**: a system can attain it only if a periodic driving force acts on it.

D is the best supported option, but B can be defended as well (a system able to resonate must have a natural frequency), so the key of the printed question is a matter of judgement and no letter is designated.

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is correct for a body giving out heat?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A body that loses thermal energy usually cools, but its temperature stays constant while it changes state (a vapour condensing, or a liquid freezing, at its fixed boiling or melting point) or if it is heated by another source at the same rate. So its temperature *could* be constant.

- A: "always drops" is false for the reason above.
- C: a body giving out heat is hotter than its surroundings, but it can still be in thermal equilibrium (no net heat flow) with another body at the same temperature.
- D: the direction of heat flow depends on the temperatures, not on the heat capacities.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Its temperature always drops with time
It cannot be in thermal equilibrium with any other body
It has a lower heat capacity than its surroundings

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is true for a body moving in a circular path at constant speed;
questions.corrige_markdown:
At constant speed the velocity changes only in direction. The acceleration $a=v^2/r=\omega^2r$ is directed towards the centre, at right angles to the velocity (tangent), so statement A is true.

- B: the magnitude of $a$ is constant but its direction turns continuously, so the acceleration vector is not constant.
- C: this is true only if "displacement" means the position vector measured from the centre of the circle; it is not true of the displacement of the body along its path. Statement A is the one that holds without any qualification.
- D: the centripetal force is whatever force points to the centre (tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction); the weight provides it only in special cases such as a satellite.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity
The acceleration is constant with time
The acceleration is always directed opposite to the displacement
The centripetal force is provided by the weight of the object

questions.enonce_markdown: When a beam of white light is incident on a diffraction grating, red light is deviated most because in the visible spectrum red light has the;
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a grating, $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, so for a given order $\sin\theta\propto\lambda$: the colour with the longest wavelength is deviated through the largest angle. Red light has the longest wavelength of the visible spectrum.

Red has the *lowest* frequency (not the highest), all colours travel at the same speed in air, and intensity is not a property that distinguishes colours.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The displacement of a particle performing simple harmonic motion with angular frequency, $\omega$, is given by $x=A\cos(\omega t-\varphi)$; where $t$ is the time and $A$ the amplitude. The total distance covered by the particle in two complete cycles is
questions.corrige_markdown:
In one complete cycle the particle goes from $+A$ to $-A$ and back: a path length of $2A+2A=4A$. In two complete cycles the distance (the total path length, not the displacement, which is zero) is $2\times4A=8A$.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If a car initially moving with a velocity of $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ accelerates steadily at $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $4$ seconds,
questions.corrige_markdown:
Given $u=4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $a=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $t=4\ \mathrm{s}$.

- Distance: $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2=4(4)+\tfrac12(2)(4)^2=16+16=32\ \mathrm{m}$, not $16\ \mathrm{m}$ (that is only the term $ut$). A is false.
- Final velocity: $v=u+at=4+2(4)=12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, not $8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. B is false.
- A steady (constant) acceleration means $v$ increases linearly with $t$: the velocity-time graph is a straight line of gradient $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which is not zero. C is true.
- D cannot be deduced from the data (it only says that the acceleration is steady).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: It covers a distance of 16 m
It attains a velocity of 8 m/s
Its velocity-time graph is a straight line with non-zero slope.
The frictional resistance to the motion is negligible.

questions.enonce_markdown: According to Coulomb's law, the force between two point charged objects is doubled if the
questions.corrige_markdown:
Coulomb's law: $F=\dfrac{kQ_1Q_2}{r^2}$.

- A: doubling each charge multiplies $Q_1Q_2$ by $4$, so $F$ is multiplied by $4$.
- B: halving the distance multiplies $1/r^2$ by $4$, so $F$ is multiplied by $4$.
- C: "closer" gives no amount, so nothing can be said.
- D: doubling the product $Q_1Q_2$ doubles $F$.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: charge on each object is doubled
product of the charges is doubled.

questions.enonce_markdown: In an electric field of strength $E$, a charge $Q$ is accelerated through a distance $y$, the work done by the electric force is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The force on the charge is $F=QE$, constant in a uniform field. Work done $=$ force $\times$ distance moved in the direction of the force $=QE\,y$. (Equivalently $W=Q\Delta V$ with $\Delta V=Ey$.)

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Images of some personalities and messages are sometimes attached to inflated balloons and the systems are observed to rise in air when released because;
questions.corrige_markdown:
A balloon is acted on by its weight (balloon, gas and the attached images) and by the upthrust of the air, equal to the weight of the air it displaces. The system rises only if the upthrust is larger than the total weight, that is, if the average density of balloon plus gas is smaller than the density of the surrounding air. Balloons filled with a light gas such as helium have a very low density compared with air ($\approx0.18$ against $\approx1.2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$).

- A: the gas inside is not warmer than the air (this is the case of hot-air balloons only).
- B: every object in air feels an upthrust; "quite significant" does not say that it exceeds the weight, so it does not explain why the system rises.
- D: the weights are not negligible; they are simply smaller than the upthrust.

C is the best explanation. The wording of B and C is loose, so this key is a judgement (see the notes).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the air inside the balloons is always warmer than the air outside
up thrust on the inflated balloons is quite significant
inflated balloons have very low densities

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 2 shows a low power lamp connected in series with a cell, V, a capacitor, C, and a switch, S, which is initially open.

![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

Which of the graphs represents the variation of the brightness of the lamp with time after the switch is closed assuming that the capacitor was initially uncharged.

![fig-3](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Just after S is closed the capacitor is uncharged, so the whole e.m.f. is across the lamp: the current is maximum, $I_0=V/R_{\text{lamp}}$, and the lamp is brightest. Charge then builds up on the capacitor, the p.d. across it rises towards $V$ and the p.d. across the lamp falls. The current decays exponentially, $I=I_0e^{-t/RC}$, to zero when the capacitor is fully charged, so the brightness (power $=I^2R$) falls steeply at first and then flattens towards zero: graph D.

- A (rising curve) would show the charge on, or the p.d. across, the capacitor.
- B: the current does not decrease linearly, its rate of fall is proportional to the current itself.
- C: a constant brightness would be obtained with a resistor only, not a capacitor in a d.c. circuit.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A beam of light of wavelength $\lambda$ ejects photoelectrons from the surface of a clean metal plate. A less intense beam of light of the same wavelength would emit photoelectrons
questions.corrige_markdown:
The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the frequency (wavelength) of the light and on the metal, $E_{k,\max}=hf-\phi$, not on the intensity. The intensity fixes the number of photons arriving per second, and so the number of photoelectrons emitted per second.

A less intense beam of the same wavelength therefore gives fewer photoelectrons, each with the same maximum kinetic energy.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: equal in number and with same KE
less in number but with same KE.
less in number and with less KE
equal in number and with less KE

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 3 shows a potentiometer used to measure the emf, $E$, of a cell. A balanced point may NOT be obtained if

![fig-4](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A balance point is found when the galvanometer reads zero, which needs the p.d. across the length $AC$ of the wire to equal the e.m.f. of the test cell: $V_{AC}=E$.

As the sliding contact C moves from A to B, $V_{AC}$ increases from $0$ to $V_{AB}$ (the p.d. across the whole wire). A balance point exists only if $E\le V_{AB}$. If $E>V_{AB}$ (the driver cell is too weak, or the wire too short or too resistive) the test cell can never be balanced, wherever C is placed.

- A and D describe the situation with C at one particular position: it only means that C is not yet at the balance point and must be moved.
- B is the balance condition itself.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The activity of a radioactive substance reduces to $68\%$ of the original value in $2.82$ hours. The half-life of the substance in hours is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Activity decays as $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$, so $0.68=e^{-\lambda(2.82)}$.

$\lambda=\dfrac{\ln(1/0.68)}{2.82}=\dfrac{0.3857}{2.82}=0.1368\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}$

$T_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln2}{\lambda}=\dfrac{0.6931}{0.1368}=5.07\ \mathrm{h}$

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Photons of light enter a glass block after travelling through a vacuum. The energy of the photons on entering the glass block
questions.corrige_markdown:
The energy of a photon is $E=hf$. The frequency is fixed by the source and does not change when the light crosses a boundary. The speed and the wavelength do change in the glass ($v=c/n$ and $\lambda=\lambda_0/n$, with $v=f\lambda$ still valid), but $f$ does not.

So the energy of the photons stays the same because the frequency does not change.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: stays the same because speed and wavelength do not change.
stays the same because frequency does not change.

questions.enonce_markdown: Laser beams are mostly very intense because
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a laser, an incoming photon causes **stimulated emission**: each excited atom that is triggered emits a photon of the same frequency, phase and direction. A very large number of such transitions take place together, so a very large number of photons in phase leave the cavity in one narrow beam, and their amplitudes add (coherence). This gives the high intensity.

- A: population inversion is the *condition* that makes this chain of stimulated emissions possible; it is not in itself the reason for the intensity.
- B and D describe the emission of light by excited atoms in general (spontaneous emission also does that, giving an ordinary weak, incoherent light).

C is the best answer. The question blends cause and condition, so this key is a judgement (see the notes).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: all electron transitions from the excited to the ground state are identical
a large number of electron transitions occur simultaneously
electrons emit energy as they fall from excited states to the ground state.

questions.enonce_markdown: A boy adds $5.00\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy to a girl on a swing by giving a push periodically each time she is at the same position of swing. After doing this continuously for $10$ minutes, a total of $2.40\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of energy has been added to her on the swing. Her frequency of swing in Hz is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The boy pushes once per cycle (each time she is at the same position of the swing), so the number of pushes equals the number of oscillations.

Number of pushes $=\dfrac{2400\ \mathrm{J}}{5.00\ \mathrm{J}}=480$ in $10\ \mathrm{min}=600\ \mathrm{s}$.

$f=\dfrac{480}{600\ \mathrm{s}}=0.80\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (period $1.25\ \mathrm{s}$).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In Ndu Tea Estate, powder tea falls from the grinding machine at a rate of $0.80\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ onto a conveyor belt moving horizontally at $2.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Determine the force in newtons needed to keep the conveyor belt moving at this constant speed.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Each second, $0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ of tea (initially with no horizontal velocity) is brought up to the speed of the belt. The force that must be supplied equals the rate of change of horizontal momentum:

$F=\dfrac{\Delta(mv)}{\Delta t}=v\,\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}=2.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\times0.80\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}=2.00\ \mathrm{N}$

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In the absence of air resistance, an object projected vertically upwards with speed, $v$ returns to the same level with speed, $v$. This is an aspect of
questions.corrige_markdown:
With no air resistance only gravity does work, so the total mechanical energy is conserved. At the starting level the kinetic energy is $\tfrac12mv^2$ going up and again $\tfrac12mv^2$ coming back (same potential energy), so the speed is the same, $v$.

Linear momentum is not conserved here (the velocity reverses and gravity is an external force), and Newton's second and third laws do not state this symmetry of speeds.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the law of conservation of linear momentum
the law of conservation of energy

questions.enonce_markdown: A car moving towards a police post at $40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ sounds its horn emitting sound of frequency $380\ \mathrm{Hz}$. If the speed of sound in air is $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the wavelength in metres of the horn as determined by the radar at the police post will be
questions.corrige_markdown:
The source moves towards the stationary observer (the police post). Successive wave crests are emitted a time $1/f_s$ apart, and during that time the source advances $v_s/f_s$, so the wavelength reaching the post is shortened:

$\lambda'=\dfrac{c-v_s}{f_s}=\dfrac{340-40}{380}=0.789\ \mathrm{m}\approx0.79\ \mathrm{m}$

Traps: $340/380=0.89$ (ignores the motion of the car) and $(340+40)/380=1.00$ (car moving away).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A beam of protons used in an experiment is referred to as being a $20\ \mathrm{MeV}$ beam. The MeV is the unit of
questions.corrige_markdown:
The electron-volt is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of one volt: $1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$. The megaelectron-volt, $1\ \mathrm{MeV}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}$, is therefore a unit of **energy**, here the kinetic energy of each proton. (The unit of potential difference is the volt, of charge the coulomb.)

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If the switch, K, in figure 4 is closed,

![fig-5](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The $20\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ and $40\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors are in series across the $6\ \mathrm{V}$ battery.

$\dfrac1C=\dfrac1{20}+\dfrac1{40}=\dfrac3{40}\ \Rightarrow\ C=13.3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ (not $60\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, which is the value for a parallel connection). A is false.

The same charge sits on both capacitors: $Q=CV=13.3\times6=80\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

- $V_{20}=Q/C=80/20=4\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_{40}=80/40=2\ \mathrm{V}$.
- B is false (the p.d. across the $40\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is $2\ \mathrm{V}$).
- C is true: in series the p.d. is inversely proportional to the capacitance, so the $20\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor has twice the p.d. ($4\ \mathrm{V}$ against $2\ \mathrm{V}$).
- D is false: $E=\tfrac12QV$ is $160\ \mu\mathrm{J}$ for the $20\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor and $80\ \mu\mathrm{J}$ for the $40\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ one.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The effective capacitance of the circuit is 60 µF.
The p.d across the 40 µF capacitor is 4 V
The p.d across the 20 µF capacitor will be double the p.d across the 40 µF capacitor.
The capacitors will each store the same amount of energy.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 shows a stone of mass $50.0\ \mathrm{g}$ tied to a $1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ long string and whirled in a vertical circle at the point where the string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the vertical.

![fig-6](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

If the stone makes $20$ revolutions in $5.00\ \mathrm{s}$. The tension in newtons on the string at this point is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Frequency $f=20/5.00=4.00\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so $\omega=2\pi f=25.1\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ (taken as constant at this point).

In the figure the stone S is below the centre, with the string at $30^\circ$ to the downward vertical. The weight $mg$ has a component $mg\cos30^\circ$ along the string, directed away from the centre. The resultant force towards the centre supplies the centripetal force:

$T-mg\cos30^\circ=m\omega^2r$

$T=m\left(\omega^2r+g\cos30^\circ\right)=0.0500\left(25.13^2\times1.50+9.81\times0.866\right)=0.0500\,(947.5+8.5)=47.8\ \mathrm{N}$

(With $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ the result is the same to three significant figures.)

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If an object is placed close to each of a thin convex and a thin concave lens perpendicularly to the principal axis such that the distance from the lens is smaller than the focal length for each case; the image formed by the
questions.corrige_markdown:
With the object **inside** the focal length:

- the convex lens (magnifying glass) forms a **virtual**, upright image that is **larger** than the object;
- the concave lens always forms a **virtual**, upright and **diminished** image.

So D is the correct statement. A is wrong because the convex lens gives a real image only when the object is beyond $f$; B and C wrongly describe the images as real.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: convex lens may either be real or virtual while the image formed by the concave lens will be virtual only
convex lens will be real and inverted while the image formed by the concave lens will be virtual and diminished
concave lens will be real and diminished while the image formed by the convex lens will be virtual and larger than the object
concave lens will be virtual and diminished while the image formed by the convex lens will be virtual and larger than the object.

questions.enonce_markdown: A parallel beam of monochromatic light of wavelength $520\ \mathrm{nm}$ is incident on a diffraction grating. The grating has $400$ lines per millimetre. The maximum order of diffraction that can be observed is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Grating spacing: $d=\dfrac{1}{400\ \mathrm{mm^{-1}}}=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mm}=2.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$.

$d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, and $\sin\theta\le1$, so $n\le\dfrac d\lambda=\dfrac{2.5\times10^{-6}}{520\times10^{-9}}=4.81$.

The order must be a whole number, so the maximum observable order is $4$ (order $5$ would need $\sin\theta=1.04>1$).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graph in figure 6 is obtained from an experiment to determine the temperature coefficient of resistance, $\alpha$, of a metal wire.

![fig-7](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

If the slope of the graph is S, then, $\alpha$ is given by
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a metal, $R=R_0(1+\alpha\theta)=R_0+R_0\alpha\,\theta$, a straight line of $R$ against $\theta$.

- Intercept on the $R$ axis: $P=R_0$ (the resistance at $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$).
- Slope: $S=R_0\alpha$.

Hence $\alpha=\dfrac{S}{R_0}=\dfrac{S}{P}$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In a heat engine, heat energy, $Q_H$ is absorbed by the engine to do mechanical work while some of the heat, $Q_C$ is not available for conversion. The efficiency of the engine is given by
questions.corrige_markdown:
Work done $W=Q_H-Q_C$. Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful work out}}{\text{heat absorbed}}=\dfrac{Q_H-Q_C}{Q_H}\times100\%=\left(1-\dfrac{Q_C}{Q_H}\right)\times100\%$.

B is the fraction of heat rejected, C and D invert the ratio and give an efficiency larger than $100\%$ or a wrong quantity.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A step down transformer with a turns ratio of $5:4$ and an efficiency of $88\%$ is used to run a motor. If the mains a.c. is $5.0\ \mathrm{A}$, the current drawn by the motor will be
questions.corrige_markdown:
The primary (mains) has $N_p:N_s=5:4$, so $V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p=4/5$. The mains current is the primary current, $I_p=5.0\ \mathrm{A}$; the motor draws the secondary current $I_s$.

Efficiency: $\eta=\dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_pI_p}=0.88\ \Rightarrow\ I_s=\eta\,I_p\,\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=0.88\times5.0\times\dfrac54=5.5\ \mathrm{A}$

(An ideal transformer would give $6.25\ \mathrm{A}$; the losses reduce it to $5.5\ \mathrm{A}$.)

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The critical angle for a ray of light moving through an optical fibre from a core of refractive index $1.54$ to a cladding of refractive index $1.48$ is approximately
questions.corrige_markdown:
Total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary begins at the critical angle $C$ with
$\sin C=\dfrac{n_{\text{cladding}}}{n_{\text{core}}}=\dfrac{1.48}{1.54}=0.961$, so $C=\sin^{-1}(0.961)=74.0^\circ$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In atomic physics the binding energy of an atomic nucleus is the
questions.corrige_markdown:
The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy that must be supplied to separate the nucleus completely into its individual, free nucleons (it is also the energy released when the nucleus is assembled, and it equals $\Delta m\,c^2$ where $\Delta m$ is the mass defect).

- A: the energy is *released*, not "used", when the nucleus forms.
- C: not a correct description.
- D: this difference of masses is the mass defect, a mass and not an energy.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: energy used in forming the nucleus from constituent nucleons
Energy needed to completely separate the nucleons
energy equivalent of the mass of the nucleus
difference between the total mass of the nucleons and that of the entire nucleus.

questions.enonce_markdown: Running water is used to remove excess heat at a rate of $120\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$ from a vacuum pump. At what rate in $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ does the water flow if it enters the pump at $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and leaves at $22\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Power removed $=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\,c\,\Delta\theta$, with $c=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ for water and $\Delta\theta=22-20=2\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{120}{4200\times2}=0.0143\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$

The options are given to two decimal places, so this is $0.01\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ (option A). The value $0.14$ is a factor of ten too large.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force of $0.60\ \mathrm{kN}$ is applied to a wire of diameter $0.002\ \mathrm{m}$ to cut it without the wire developing a 'neck'. Find the breaking stress in Pa on the wire.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Stress $=\dfrac{F}{A}$ with $F=0.60\ \mathrm{kN}=600\ \mathrm{N}$ and the cross-section $A=\dfrac{\pi d^2}{4}=\dfrac{\pi(0.002)^2}{4}=3.14\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

$\sigma=\dfrac{600}{3.14\times10^{-6}}=1.9\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{Pa}$

The value $4.8\times10^7\ \mathrm{Pa}$ (option C) comes from using the diameter as if it were the radius ($A=\pi d^2$).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A newly discovered planet has a mass equal to one eighth the mass of the earth and a radius equal to half of the earth's radius. If the gravitational field strength on the earth's surface is $g$, the gravitational field strength on the new planet's surface is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$g=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$. For the new planet, $M'=M/8$ and $R'=R/2$:

$g'=\dfrac{G(M/8)}{(R/2)^2}=\dfrac{GM}{8}\cdot\dfrac{4}{R^2}=\dfrac{GM}{2R^2}=\dfrac g2$

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $^{214}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}$ decays by a series of transformations emitting $2$ alpha particles and $4$ beta particles to a final stable product. Which of the following could be the symbol for the stable nucleus formed?
questions.corrige_markdown:
- Each alpha particle ($^4_2\mathrm{He}$) lowers the nucleon number by $4$ and the proton number by $2$: two alphas give $A=214-8=206$ and $Z=82-4=78$.
- Each beta-minus particle raises $Z$ by $1$ (a neutron becomes a proton) and leaves $A$ unchanged: four betas give $Z=78+4=82$.

The final nucleus is $^{206}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}$. A and B keep $A=214$ (impossible after emitting alpha particles) and D has the wrong nucleon number $208$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 7 below shows a coil connected in series with a resistor and a battery

![fig-8](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

When K is closed?

1. The initial increase in current is $5.2\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}$
2. The maximum current in L is $1.2\ \mathrm{A}$
3. The back emf across the coil drops with time

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the coil as having negligible resistance.

1. At $t=0$ the current is zero, so there is no p.d. across the resistor and the whole e.m.f. is across the coil: $L\dfrac{dI}{dt}=12.0\ \mathrm{V}$, hence $\dfrac{dI}{dt}=\dfrac{12.0}{2.3}=5.2\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}$. **True.**
2. When the current has become steady the back e.m.f. is zero and $I_{\max}=\dfrac{V}{R}=\dfrac{12.0}{10.0}=1.2\ \mathrm{A}$. **True.**
3. The back e.m.f. $\mathcal E=L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$ is $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ at the start and falls to zero as the growth of the current slows down. **True.**

All three statements are correct, but none of the printed options (1 and 2; 2 and 3; 1 only; 3 only) is "1, 2 and 3". The question is defective, so no letter is designated.

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The slope of a velocity - time graph for a car gives

1. its rate of change of momentum with time
2. its acceleration
3. the resultant force per unit mass acting on it.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration, $a=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ (statement 2 is true). By Newton's second law $a=\dfrac{F_{\text{net}}}{m}$, so it is also the resultant force per unit mass (statement 3 is true).

The rate of change of momentum is $\dfrac{\Delta(mv)}{\Delta t}=ma$, the resultant *force*, not the slope (statement 1 is false).

Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A small magnetic needle in a compass is at rest on a horizontal table top in a science laboratory. Which of the following may cause deflection of the needle?

1. A straight wire carrying current
2. A collimated beam of beta particles
3. An intense LASER beam of monochromatic light
questions.corrige_markdown:
A compass needle is deflected by a steady magnetic field.

1. A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it: it deflects the needle.
2. A beam of beta particles is a stream of moving charges, that is an electric current: it produces a magnetic field and deflects the needle.
3. A laser beam is an electromagnetic wave whose magnetic field oscillates at about $10^{14}$ to $10^{15}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ with zero average; the needle cannot follow such fast reversals, so there is no deflection.

Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If the oscillations accompanying the propagation of a wave can be restricted to a single plane then it can be deduced that the wave could be;

1. transverse
2. electromagnetic
3. longitudinal
questions.corrige_markdown:
Oscillations that can be confined to one plane (plane polarisation) are possible only for waves whose oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel, i.e. transverse waves (statement 1). Electromagnetic waves are transverse (electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to the direction of travel) and can be polarised (statement 2). The oscillations of a longitudinal wave lie along the direction of travel, so they cannot be restricted to a plane in this way (statement 3 is false).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The resistance of a piece of copper wire varies with

1. resistivity
2. thickness
3. length

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
$R=\dfrac{\rho L}{A}$: the resistance is proportional to the length $L$ (statement 3) and inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area $A$, i.e. to the square of the thickness (statement 2). The resistivity $\rho$ is also in the formula (statement 1): it is a property of the material that changes with temperature, but for a given piece of copper at a fixed temperature it is a constant.

If "varies with" is taken literally (every quantity in the formula), all three statements are correct, which is not an option. If it means the quantities that can be changed for a given piece of copper wire, only 2 and 3 are correct. The second reading is the more likely intention of the question.

**Intended answer: B (2 and 3 are correct).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following is/are conservative forces?

1. gravitational force
2. tension
3. friction
questions.corrige_markdown:
A force is conservative if the work it does between two points is independent of the path and if it can be associated with a potential energy.

1. Gravity is conservative: the work depends only on the change of height, and there is a gravitational potential energy.
2. The tension in a string or rope is a constraint force which is not derived from a potential energy and is not classified as conservative.
3. Friction is not conservative: the work done depends on the length of the path and energy is dissipated as heat.

Only statement 1 is correct.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two identical copper wires A and B carrying currents of magnitudes $2.5\ \mathrm{A}$ and $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$ respectively in the same direction are placed on a table $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart. Which of the following is/are true?

1. Force of B on A is greater than force of A on B
2. The force between them will be attractive.
3. The magnetic flux of A through B is less than that of B through A
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. By Newton's third law the two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. Each wire feels $F=\dfrac{\mu_0I_AI_B}{2\pi d}L$ per length $L$, whatever the individual currents. **False.**
2. Parallel currents in the same direction attract each other: the field of one wire acts on the other wire with a force towards it. **True.**
3. The flux linked with one wire due to the other is proportional to the current producing it (through the same mutual geometry): that of A through B is proportional to $2.5\ \mathrm{A}$ and that of B through A to $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$, so the first is the smaller. **True.**

Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The potential energy between a pair of molecules of a substance can be increased by

1. bringing them closer
2. cooling the substance
3. moving them apart

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
The potential energy of a pair of molecules is lowest at the equilibrium separation $r_0$. Moving the molecules apart (3) increases it, because work is done against the attractive force. Pushing them closer than $r_0$ (1) also increases it, steeply, because of the repulsive force. Cooling the substance (2) mainly lowers the kinetic energy of the molecules and does not by itself raise the potential energy.

So statement 3 is true, and statement 1 is also true if the molecules start at or inside the equilibrium separation. As statement 1 depends on the starting separation, and "1 and 3" is not an option, the key is open to interpretation. The usual textbook idea is that the intermolecular potential energy rises when molecules are pulled apart (as when a solid melts or a liquid boils).

**Intended answer: D (3 only is correct).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Nuclear fusion could be better than nuclear fission in harnessing nuclear energy and converting it to useful forms because

1. fission occurs very slowly
2. fusion yields more energy than fission for equal masses of fuel
3. fuel for fusion is easily obtainable
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. Fission is a fast chain reaction which has to be slowed and controlled in a reactor; it is not slow. **False.**
2. Per unit mass of fuel, fusion of light nuclei releases more energy than fission of heavy nuclei (for example about $3.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon for deuterium-tritium fusion against about $0.85\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon for uranium-235 fission). **True.**
3. The fuel of fusion (deuterium, extracted from sea water, and tritium made from lithium) is abundant, whereas uranium ore is limited. **True.**

Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 8 shows a bridge circuit of 4 resistors.

![fig-9](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

1. P.d across AB $=6\ \mathrm{V}$
2. $I=0.6\ \mathrm{A}$
3. $R=3\ \Omega$

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the figure the cell is connected across the top and bottom corners of the bridge, and the galvanometer G joins the side corners A and B.

The text does not say that the bridge is balanced. If it is (zero reading on G, so $V_A=V_B$), the resistances in the two arms are in the same ratio: $\dfrac{12}{24}=\dfrac{R}{6}$, so $R=3\ \Omega$ (statement 3 is true). Then:

- The p.d. across AB is zero, not $6\ \mathrm{V}$ (statement 1 is false; AB is the galvanometer branch, so $6\ \mathrm{V}$ is not possible whatever $R$ is).
- The two arms in parallel draw $I=\dfrac{6}{12+24}+\dfrac{6}{3+6}=0.167+0.667=0.83\ \mathrm{A}$, not $0.6\ \mathrm{A}$ (statement 2 is false).

Only statement 3 is correct, which would be option D. This relies on an assumption that the printed question does not give.

**Intended answer: D (3 only is correct).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = the gravitational field strength at a point on the surface of a planet, and $x$ = the mean radius of the planet.

![fig-10](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

*Options as printed:* A) straight line through the origin, rising   B) falling curve (like a hyperbola) that is steep at small $x$ and flattens   C) straight line decreasing from a positive value on the $y$-axis   D) straight line rising from the origin to a peak, then a falling curve
questions.corrige_markdown:
At the surface, $g=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$. The answer depends on what is kept constant when the radius changes, which the question does not say:

- **Same mass $M$:** $g\propto1/R^2$, a falling curve: graph B.
- **Same mean density $\rho$:** $M=\tfrac43\pi R^3\rho$, so $g=\tfrac43\pi G\rho R\propto R$, a straight line through the origin: graph A.

Graph C is not given by either case. Graph D is the variation of $g$ with the distance $r$ from the centre of one uniform planet (rising linearly inside, falling as $1/r^2$ outside), which is not a graph against the radius of different planets.

Two graphs are defensible, so no letter is designated.

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = number of radioactive nuclei of a radioactive substance already decayed, and $x$ = time of decay.

![fig-11](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_11.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
If $N_0$ nuclei are present at $t=0$, the number left is $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and the number already decayed is
$N_d=N_0-N=N_0\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)$.

This is zero at $t=0$, rises most rapidly at the start (the activity is greatest then) and flattens off towards $N_0$ as the sample is used up: graph C. Graph D is the number of undecayed nuclei, A is a straight-line fall and B an accelerating rise.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = mean square speed of gas molecules, and $x$ = absolute temperature of the gas.

![fig-12](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
For an ideal gas, $\tfrac12m\langle c^2\rangle=\tfrac32kT$, so $\langle c^2\rangle=\dfrac{3kT}{m}$: the mean square speed is directly proportional to the absolute temperature. The graph is a straight line through the origin: graph A.

(The r.m.s. speed, $\sqrt{\langle c^2\rangle}$, would give a curve flattening with $T$.)

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = kinetic energy of a child on a swing, and $x$ = displacement from the rest position.

![fig-13](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a swing (simple harmonic motion of amplitude $A$) the displacement $x$ is measured on both sides of the rest position. The kinetic energy is
$E_k=\tfrac12k\left(A^2-x^2\right)$: maximum at $x=0$ (rest position, highest speed) and zero at $x=\pm A$ (the ends of the swing). The graph is an inverted parabola, symmetrical about the $y$-axis and cutting the $x$-axis at $\pm A$: graph C.

Graph D (U-shaped) is the graph of the potential energy, A and B do not have this shape.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = the acceleration of a ball kicked vertically upwards, and $x$ = time until the ball reaches maximum height.

![fig-14](gce-al-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_14.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Once the ball has left the foot, the only force on it (neglecting air resistance) is its weight. The acceleration is therefore constant, $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ directed downwards, all the way up and at the top. With upward taken as positive this is a constant negative value: a horizontal line **below** the time axis, graph C.

A (increasing) and B (changing sign) would mean a changing acceleration. D is also a constant but above the axis, which would be the case only if downward were taken as positive, so it is not the usual choice.

**Answer: C.**
